newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Blair hunts for perfect photo-op.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Blair hunts for perfect photo-op.

text.p: Shock horror. Toddlers cheat death as Tony Blair's river boat capsizes.

It didn't happen, of course, but the wrinkled brow of the Labour leader's normally unflappable press secretary, Alistair Campbell, spoke volumes of the potential disasters that could have wrecked his election campaign at a stroke on Wednesday.

Blair came to Bristol in western England for a photo-opportunity -- nothing more, nothing less. He made no speeches, held no meetings, went on no walkabouts and shook hands with perhaps a few dozen voters.
But in an election where the television "bite" and nice photo are as important as the battle of ideas, nothing was left to chance in lining up the best camera angles and most photogenic settings.
A news agency reporter chosen to accompany Blair on his boat was even asked to leave her brown coat behind in order not to spoil the image of the Labour leader smiling in the spring sunshine.
"We keep trying to capture the interest of voters who are following the election on TV or in the newspapers. We want to provide variety," one of Blair's senior aides explained.
After taking the train to Bristol, about 50 reporters and cameramen travel ahead of Blair to Bristol's maritime heritage centre and clamber aboard a press launch to await his arrival.
Campbell nervously checks the narrow boat, the Redshank, that Blair is to board with a class of local primary school children.

As a small army of minders, press stewards and local party officials scurry about, a waving Blair duly arrives and steps on to the 6-foot wide boat with his wife Cherie, who has prudently slipped into canvas boat shoes for the short ride.

The Redshank pushes off into the dirty brown waters of the River Avon before circling round to give photographers the picturesque background of an old sailing ship -- much better than the rusting gasholders and disused warehouses on the opposite bank.
Blair, by now in his shirtsleeves, waves, waves and waves again. So do his schoolchildren props. Only Campbell still looks uneasy.
Then it is off down the river for a 15-minute cruise, more waves and a quick word for the cameras as the Labour leader disembarks.
"The campaign's going excellently so far, but we have to take nothing for granted," he says.
With a smile, he hops on his bus and is gone. Nothing has happened. His people are pleased.
